We have conducted multiple public goods game experiments with varying experimental designs, to measure the effect of costly punishment in cooperative settings under various environments.
            Your task is to predict how enabling a punishment mechanism to a specific game changes the ***efficiency*** compared to the same game with punishment disabled.
            According to our experiments, whether and how much punishment increases efficiency or not is highly dependent on a lot of dimensions in experiment design, and it is your job to navigate this heterogeneity and make accurate predictions.

            ***Efficiency*** is the ratio between the game player's behavior and that of a fully-cooperative group (i.e. a group in which all members contribute their full endowment in every round)
            In other words, efficiency measures how close a group's total payoff is, compared to that of an ideal group that always cooperates without paying any cost (i.e. always contributes the entire endowment, and benefits maximally from the multiplier). 
            An efficiency value of 100% means that a group earned the same amount of coins as a hypothetical group that always cooperated without cost from punishment or reward.
            
            For example, let's say a game has 5 players playing 10 rounds where 20 coins are given to each player per round and the multiplier for each contributed coin is 3.
            In this case, the earning of a hypothetical "always cooperating" group without punishment is 5*10*20*3=3000 coins, while the earning of a hypothetical "never cooperating" group without punishment is 1000 coins.
            Hence, the efficiency is 1 for the always cooperating group and 0.33 for the never cooperating group.
